A **finite discrete memoryless channel (DMC)** is the channel sequence [[def-channel-sequence]] with fixed finite nonempty input and output alphabets $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ (with every subset measurable) and one stochastic kernel $W(y\mid x)$ from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ ([[def-finite-stochastic-kernel]]). At every blocklength its input and output alphabets are $\mathcal X^n,\mathcal Y^n$, and its block kernel is
$$W^n(y^n\mid x^n):=\prod_{i=1}^n W(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Thus the same single-use transition law is applied independently at each coordinate, conditional on the input word. This page imposes no feedback or input-cost constraint.

Let $\mathcal X,\mathcal Y$ be finite nonempty sets. A **stochastic kernel**
from $\mathcal X$ to $\mathcal Y$ is a matrix
$K=(K(y\mid x))_{x\in\mathcal X,y\in\mathcal Y}$ such that
$K(y\mid x)\ge0$ and $\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y}K(y\mid x)=1$ for every
$x\in\mathcal X$. The convention is input first in the condition and output
first in the value $K(y\mid x)$.

For a probability vector $P=(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, the output vector
$PK$ on $\mathcal Y$ is
$$(PK)_y:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_xK(y\mid x).$$
It is a probability vector because its coordinates are nonnegative and
$\sum_y(PK)_y=\sum_xp_x\sum_yK(y\mid x)=\sum_xp_x=1$.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. $$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

For every $\alpha>0$,
$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{\log x}{x^\alpha}=0.$$

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln M_n}{n}\ge R,\qquad \varepsilon_{\rm av}(n)\longrightarrow0.$$
It is **maximal-error achievable** if the same condition holds with $\varepsilon_{\max}(n)\to0$. Define $C_{\rm av}(W)$ and $C_{\max}(W)$ as the suprema of the respective achievable-rate sets. Rates use nats per channel use.

For an input probability vector $P_X$ on $\mathcal X$ ([[def-finite-probability-vector]]), let $P_{XY}(x,y):=P_X(x)W(y\mid x)$ and $Q_{P_X}(y):=\sum_xP_X(x)W(y\mid x)$. Write $I(P_X;W):=I(X;Y)$ for this joint law, using [[def-it-finite-mutual-information]]. The **single-letter information capacity** is
$$C(W):=\sup_{P_X} I(P_X;W),$$
measured in nats per channel use. The finite-dimensional maximum is attained, as proved in [[lem-discrete-memoryless-channel-capacity-is-attained]].

Every length-$n$ code with average error $\varepsilon_{\rm av}$ has a subcode with at least $M/2$ messages and maximal error at most $2\varepsilon_{\rm av}$.

derivations.claim: A maximal-error reliable sequence is also average-error reliable because $\varepsilon_{\rm av}\le\varepsilon_{\max}$. Thus [F3] gives $C_{\max}(W)\le C_{\rm av}(W)\le C(W)$.

By [F4], every $0\le R<C(W)$ is average-error achievable, so $C_{\rm av}(W)\ge C(W)$ after taking the supremum when $C(W)>0$. If $C(W)=0$, [F7] gives $C_{\rm av}(W)\ge0$. The case split is exhaustive by [F6]; in either case $C_{\rm av}(W)=C(W)$.

If $C(W)>0$, fix any $0\le R<C(W)$. By [F4] there is an average-error reliable sequence at rate at least $R$. Apply [F5] to each code: the maximal errors tend to zero and the log message count loses at most $\ln2$ at blocklength $n$, so the resulting rate is still at least $R$ in the limit. Thus $C_{\max}(W)\ge R$ for every such $R$, and hence $C_{\max}(W)\ge C(W)$. If $C(W)=0$, [F7] gives $C_{\max}(W)\ge0=C(W)$. The cases are exhaustive by [F6], and step 1.1 gives equality.
